idiom_name: callable stored or passed as the strategy (plain function, partial, or callable object)
implementation_notes: A strategy in Python is any callable: a plain function, a bound method, a functools.partial with its configuration bound, or an object implementing __call__. The standard library already takes strategies this way - sorted/min/max take the key function, itertools and heapq accept key/cmp helpers, and functools.cmp_to_key adapts a comparison-style strategy to the key-style API - so the classic ABC-plus-subclasses structure is only justified when the strategy carries configuration that deserves a name (a dataclass with __call__), groups several operations, or must be enforced as a contract at a plugin boundary (typing.Protocol or abc.ABC). functools.partial is the closure-free way to bind configuration to a function and is usually the whole configured-strategy implementation.
pitfalls: A bound method or closure keeps its owner alive: storing one on a long-lived context can pin the object it was bound to and its whole reference graph for as long as the context lives.
Functions are mutable objects: setting attributes on a strategy function, or relying on module-level state it reads, makes behaviour depend on shared global mutation and breaks independent tests.

A wrong-arity or wrong-signature callable is accepted by the type checker unless a Callable/Protocol annotation (or a runtime check) describes it, and fails only when the call happens - Protocol plus @runtime_checkable documents the contract.
